newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: PARKS SERVICE WAS AWARE OF ROAD'S INSTABILITY
The National Parks and Wildlife has been aware the Alpine Way road to the Thredbo ski village has been unstable for some time.
Sections of the road way have been slipping for more than ten years.
The Alpine Way has been natorious for being unstable but mainly in sections away from Thredbo village.
For example, in 1993 there were a total of 28 land slips along the 22 kilometre stretch of road.
The then Coalition government allocated $5-million over five years to upgrade and stabalise the road.
It was part of the Ski 2000 program aimed at increasing tourist beds into the area by almost 1,000 and assisting with access for skiers to the slopes.
The ABC understands while there were some sections in the village area that needed repair there were no major indications a section abutting the roadway was in danger of collapse.
HUMAN CHAIN REMOVES DEBRIS AT LANDSLIDE SITE
In the New South Wales Snowy Mountains, rescue work has begun at the site of a landslide which it's feared has buried up to 20 people.

Just on 12-hours after the landslide buried two ski lodges at Thredbo ski village, rescue workers have moved onto the site. They've formed a human chain and are removing sections of debris piece by piece using heavy hammers to break up large concrete slabs.
The start to the work follows an inspection of the site by a geo-physicist flown to Thredbo this morning.
A large amount of machinery, including excavators and cranes has been brought to the site.
An Ambulance Spokeswoman says witnesses heard voices coming from the chalet this morning.
New South Wales Premier Bob Carr has discussed the tragedy with Acting Prime Minister, Peter Costello, who's pledged Commonwealth assistance in the rescue effort.
Mr Carr says he is making plans to visit the rescue site with State Police Commissioner, Peter Ryan, tomorrow.
The Federal Opposition Leader Kim Beazley says the prayers of the nation are with the missing people and their families.
"I think all of us are praying very much for the deft hand for the rescuers and for courage and good spirits for those who may still be trapped," Mr Beazley said.
"And of course comfort and condolences to the realtives of those who who may be dead," he said.
HIGH COURT JUDGEMENT ON FREEDOM OF SPEECH
The High court has reinforced its position on freedom of speech on political matters, in a judgement on Victorian laws.
Victoria's laws on duck-hunting were challenged as unconstitutional.
The laws regulate media and protestor access to the wetlands during the duck hunting season.
The anti duck-hunting lobby argued they breached a 1994 High court ruling, that the Federal Constitution contained an implied right to free speech on political matters.
But a High court composed of different judges largely overturned that ruling earlier this month, and it reinforced its position in a unanimous judgement in this case.
That means free speech on political issues is still only protected from defamation action in certain situations.
Victorian anti duck-hunting campaigner Laurie levy says he's disappointed but not surprised at the ruling, and his fight will continue.
PARK MANAGER SAYS OVERDEVELOPMENT DIDN'T CAUSE LANDSLIP
The Manager of the Snowy Mountains National Park says overdevelopment of the Thredbo village or poor roads' maintenance are not behind this morning's disaster.
Greg Manson says it appears to have been a natural landslip.
He says the National Parks and Wildlife Service follows the same national standards for approving resort developments as local councils.
Mr Manson says the Alpine Way has been regularly monitored and upgraded since it first slipped in 1978.
"The slips have previously occurred right in this area," he said.
"The road is constantly being upgraded and we have special monitoring devices in the road which help us determine whether there's any water or landslips in the area."
Mr Manson said there were no warnings from the monitoring devices that he was aware of.
PROSPECTS IMPROVE FOR HEROIN TRIAL AS MINISTERS MEET
The Federal Health Minister, Michael Wooldridge, believes there is still a chance the heroin trial in the ACT will go ahead.
The issue will be discussed during a two day Health Ministers meeting in Cairns which begins today.
The Federal Minister says there was discussions about the trial during a dinner last night, and the prospects are more positive.
Dr Wooldridge has told Radio National the key has been looking at other heroin substitutes and that is very important.
"Victoria has been very strongly pushing the notion of trialling a number of other heroin substitutes and there are a number of substitutes. I think that will probably get up," Dr Wooldridge said.
"I would like though to see something co-ordinated between the States, not all States doing different things and I think that's our challenge this morning," he said.
SUICIDE AND BULLYING LINKED: STUDY
A South Australian study has found a link between teenage suicide or suicide attempts, and bullying.
Professor Ken Rigby from the University of South Australia, says it's the first time such a link has been established.
The study involved more than 800 boys and nearly 700 girls aged between 11 and 17.
Professor Rigby says the bullying could cause serious depression and poor health in both the victim and the perpetrator.
Also contributing to the problems were perceptions of not being cared for by parents, or supported by peers and teachers at school.
Professor Rigby says most students are resilient to bullying but a minority of victims and bullies are seriously disturbed and schools should address it.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
